adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The provincial archive occupies a converted grain warehouse near the canal, and its reading room opens to the public four days each week. Visitors sign a register, leave their coats on hooks, and carry only pencils and notebooks into the collection. The staff have spent eleven years cataloguing the ledgers of the old shipping companies, a collection that fills nearly two hundred shelves. Each volume records cargo, dates, wages, and the names of captains, clerks, and dockworkers. The paper has yellowed, and the ink has faded along the windows. Conservators repair torn pages with wheat paste and thin tissue, a slow process that consumes most of their budget. Researchers requesting boxes wait a day, and staff retrieve each box themselves. The basement was dug in 1912, and its brick walls still carry the marks of the original builders. A narrow staircase connects it to the loading bay, and a second door leads into the courtyard. In summer the courtyard hosts small concerts and a market selling honey, bread, and secondhand books. The archive's director, a historian named Marta Feld, has argued that local records deserve the same attention as national collections. Her own research concerns the grain trade and the families behind it, and she has published two books and a long series of articles on the subject. School groups visit twice a month, and the staff prepare worksheets, quizzes, and short talks about the building's history. Funding comes mostly out of a regional trust and the sale of reproductions, postcards, and guidebooks.
The reading room itself is plain: long oak tables, green lamps, a clock above the door, and a notice asking readers to keep their voices low. Photocopying is limited to a few pages per request, and photography without flash is allowed. The catalogue was typed on index cards in 2008, and a volunteer team later entered every card into a database. Errors remain, and the staff welcome corrections. A small exhibition in the entrance hall displays maps, photographs, and tools of the warehouse's working years. The exhibition changes twice a year, and local collectors lend most of the objects. Attendance has grown steadily, and the director hopes to extend the opening hours with new funds.
During the winter of 2019, a storm tore away part of the roof, and water dripped onto the shelves below. Under Feld's supervision, the damaged volumes were moved into a dry room and laid out on trestle tables. No one could say how well the ink would survive the drying process, and several pages had already lost their colour. The board decided that all future repairs should be recorded in a separate register, and that a copy should be sent to the national library. Whenever a box is requested now, a conservator checks the pages first; throughout the summer, volunteers worked beneath the repaired roof to clear the last of the dust. Visitors often ask whether the archive has recovered, and the answer is that most of the collection is once again available.
